spec:
# Claim concepts: attribution of the claim's concept, with and without the credited pieces

Draft for review. Nothing has run.

**Measure.** Integrated gradients through the /encoder0/ln2 decoder (square_attribution.py --ig 32), per bit.
A concept's attribution = sum over its bits, signed for the side named. Two kinds of test:

- **With / without**: the quote credits a piece (or a move) with the concept. The concept's attribution on the real
  board vs the board with that piece taken off (or the move taken back). Each credited piece separately. Reported raw
  and as a share of the board's total |attribution|, because taking material off shifts every attribution.
- **Descriptive**: the quote only states the concept. Its attribution for the named side, against the same concept
  for the other side where the quote compares them.

Squares are real-board squares.

## Concepts (bit sets)

| concept | bits |
|---|---|
| Space(X, files) | X's `control.reach.t`, `control.geometry.t` with t in the opponent's half (on those files), plus `square.control.X*` on those t |
| Centre(X) | same, t in d4 e4 d5 e5 |
| Hold(X, s) | X's control bits targeting s, `square.control.X*` and `strong.X.*` on s |
| Outpost(s) | `strong.<owner>.*` on s, `stability.*` on s (an enemy pawn or piece can hit it), `role.protected_by` on s |
| KingSafety(K) | on K's square and its 8 neighbours: `pawn_shield.*`, `king.castle`, `pawn_cover.<owner>*`, `square.control.*`; the enemy's control bits targeting them; `role.attacks` bits naming K |
| KingMobility(K) | K's `mobility.*`, `control.*`, `blocked_by.own.*` |
| Pair(X) | `bishop_pair.*`, `unlike_bishops.*` on X's bishops |
| Activity(piece) | the piece's `control.*`, `mobility.*`, `xray.*`, `role.*` |
| Passer(p) | `pawn.passed`, `pawn.rank4_6`, `pawn.rank7` on p; `role.protected_by` on p; `rook.behind_passer` naming p |
| Threat(s) | `threat.*` on s |
| Weakness(pawns) | `pawn.isolated`, `pawn.doubled_with.*`, `pawn.hanging`, `weak.<owner>` on the pawns' squares; `role.attacks` and `stability.*` naming them; for 25 also the owner's `role.defends` bits naming them (pieces tied down) |

## With / without

| # | claim | concept | taken off / back | expected |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | W space: two centre pawns, knight on the 4th | Space(W) | Pe4, Pf4, Nd4 | drops for each |
| 2 | B space: e4, f5, knight e5 | Space(B) | pe4, pf5, ne5 | drops for each (ne5: −0.039 raw, done) |
| 3 | W space: d5, f4, queen d4 | Space(W) | Pd5, Pf4, Qd4 | drops for each |
| 4 | B space on the queenside | Space(B, a–d) | pb4, pc3 | drops for each |
| 5 | B cramped on the queen's wing | Activity of B's pieces on a–d (mobility only) | Pa3, Pb4, Pc4, Pd5 | rises for each |
| 13 | ...b4 supports the c3 knight | Outpost(c3) | pb4 | drops |
| 14 + 40 | unassailable Nf4; B's bishops have little to say | Pair(B) | Nf4 | rises |
| 15 | W cannot castle (...Bh3) | KingSafety(Ke1) incl. `king.castle` | bd7 | rises |
| 16 | O-O-O brought W's king into safety | KingSafety(W king) | take 12.O-O-O back (Ke1, Ra1) | lower before |
| 19 | ...h6 weakened B's king | KingSafety(kg8) | take ...h6 back (pawn to h7) | higher before |
| 22 | d6 threatens d7 and Qd6+ | Threat(d6), Passer(d6) | Qd3 | drops |
| 23 | protected passed pawn | Passer(g5) | Pf4 (the protector) | drops |
| 30 | B king more mobile, W king hampered by own pawns | KingMobility(Kg1) | Pf2, Pg2, Ph2 | rises |
| 32 | rook cuts the B king off | KingMobility(kf8), signed for Black | Rh7 | rises |

## Descriptive

| # | claim | concept | expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | W dominates the centre | Centre(W) vs Centre(B) | W > 0, W > B |
| 7 | B superior in the centre | Centre(B) vs Centre(W) | B > 0, B > W |
| 8 + 43 | d5 secured for B | Hold(B, d5) | > 0 |
| 9 + 12 | B's two bishops; strongly posted ne4 | Pair(B), Outpost(e4) | both > 0 |
| 10 | W's bishops decisive; B's knights lack bases | Pair(W); Outpost(nd7), Outpost(ne5) | Pair(W) > 0; outposts ≤ 0 |
| 11 | two bishops beat bishop and knight | Pair(B) + Activity(ba6, bb6) vs Activity(Bb4, Nc6) | B > W |
| 17 | B forced to weaken the kingside | KingSafety(kg8), signed for Black | < 0 |
| 18 | W king exposed, B king entrenched | KingSafety(Kg2), KingSafety(kg8) | W < 0, B > 0 |
| 20 | W king exposed | KingSafety(Kd2) | < 0 |
| 21 | W passed pawn, commanding king | Passer(e4), Activity(Ke3) | both > 0 |
| 24 | three isolated pawns, attacked | Weakness(a5, d6, f5), signed for Black | < 0 |
| 25 | isolated pawns tied to pieces | Weakness(a5, c7, e5, e6) incl. defenders | < 0 |
| 26 | doubled c-pawn | Weakness(c6, c7) | < 0 |
| 27 | extra pawn doubled, of no account | `material.up` + Weakness(c4, c6), signed for Black | sum ≈ 0 |
| 28 | isolated d5 weak | Weakness(d5) | < 0 |
| 29 | isolated h7 weak | Weakness(h7) | < 0 |
| 31 | W commands the 7th; e3 isolated, g2 backward | `rook.seventh` + Activity(Ra7); Weakness(e3, g2) | > 0; < 0 |
| 33 | ra2 out of play | Activity(ra2) | ≈ 0 |
| 39 | B's queenside space not real | Space(B, a–c) + Weakness(b4, c5, a6) | sum ≤ 0 |
| 41 | bb7 inactive, keeping the pair a mistake | Activity(bb7); Pair(B) | ≈ 0; ≤ 0 |
| 42 | Nd5 can't be maintained | `stability.*` on d5, signed for White | < 0 |

## Gaps

- **Development (34–38):** no bits encode development (moves spent, pieces off the back rank). Drop, or add a feature.
- **Backward pawn (31's g2):** no `backward` bit; Weakness has only isolated/doubled/hanging and the attacks.
- **Absences:** "unassailable" (14) and "lack bases" (10) are the *absence* of `stability.*` / `strong.*` bits, and
  attribution can't credit a bit that isn't there. 14 is tested through the with/without on Pair(B) instead.
- **"≈ 0" and "> 0" thresholds** for descriptive claims are not fixed yet.

claim: White has more space: two centre pawns and a knight on the fourth rank.
games.quote: Force and time on both sides are alike; the difference is only in space. White has two centre Pawns and a Knight on the fourth rank, while Black has all his pieces on the first three ranks.
games.source: Znosko-Borovsky, The Middle Game in Chess (1922), Superior Positions, Advantage in Space, Diagram LXIII; Lasker – Capablanca, St Petersburg 1914, after 10...Re8

claim: Black has gained space with pawns on e4 and f5 and the knight on e5.
games.quote: As regards space, Black has undoubtedly gained, thanks to his advanced Pawns on [e4] and [f5] and the Knight on [e5]. White has only one Pawn on the fourth rank ([c4]), all his other men being crowded together on the first three ranks.
games.source: Znosko-Borovsky, The Middle Game in Chess (1922), Valuation of the Position, Diagram XLIII; Vergani – Teichmann, Hastings 1895, after 21...Ne5

claim: White has gained space with pawns on d5 and f4 and the queen on d4.
games.quote: We can further easily see that White has gained also in space, because his Pawns stand on [d5] and [f4], and the Queen on [d4], while Black has all his pieces posted on three ranks.
games.source: Znosko-Borovsky, The Middle Game in Chess (1922), Valuation of the Position, Diagram XLII; Leonhardt – Marshall, San Sebastian 1911, after 15...Rad8

claim: Black's lead in time has become a lead in space on the queenside.
games.quote: Only his advantage in time has turned into advantage in space, for he has succeeded in advancing his Queen's side Pawns, bringing one of them to the sixth rank.
games.source: Znosko-Borovsky, The Middle Game in Chess (1922), Construction and Execution of the Plan, Diagram LII; Pillsbury – Tarrasch, Hastings 1895, after 31...c3

claim: Black is much cramped on the queen's wing.
games.quote: The diversion of the [knight], now completed, has so altered the situation that Black, though much cramped on the Q’s Wing, can venture to proceed to the attack!
games.source: Nimzowitsch, My System (1930), Part II, Elements of Position Play, § 6 over-protection of the centre, Diagram CXXIII; Opocensky – Nimzowitsch, Marienbad 1925, after 16...c6

claim: ...b4 supports Black's knight on c3 and gives Black winning chances.
games.quote: The continuation of the game shows that the text-move offers Black a chance of victory, by allowing him to support his [knight on c3] by [...b4] on his 29th move.
games.source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 70, note to White's 20th move; Rubinstein – Alekhine, London 1922, after 29...b4

claim: White's unassailable knight on f4 outweighs the two bishops.
Black's two bishops have little to say against White's unassailable knight.
games.quote: White has the better game, for the two [bishops] have little to say in view of the strength of the unassailable [knight]
games.source: Nimzowitsch, My System (1930), Part II ch. 5 (Over-protection), position after Diagram CLXVI (Game No. 15), text after 19. Kt-B4; Nimzowitsch – von Freymann, Wilna 1912, after 19.Nf4

claim: White cannot castle and is in a very difficult position.
games.quote: White already finds himself in a very difficult position, since he cannot Castle on account of 18...[Bh3], winning the Exchange.
games.source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 64, position after Black's 17th move; Johner – Alekhine, Pistyan 1922, after 17...Qg6

claim: 12.O-O-O brings White's king into safety.
games.quote: In addition to the attacking probabilities of the text move, White in one move brings his King into safety and brings one of his Rooks into play.
games.source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), ch. VI, Game 4, note to White's 12th move; Capablanca – Znosko-Borovsky, St Petersburg 1913, after 12.O-O-O

claim: 8...h6 has weakened Black's king position.
games.quote: The anxiety to provide against [Ng5] or [Bg5] is natural enough, but the resultant weakening of the King’s position may have unfortunate consequences, as the bad development of the Black pieces does not warrant this move.
games.source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 9, note to Black's 8th move; Alekhine – Marco, Stockholm 1912, after 8...h6

claim: White's passed d6 pawn threatens d7 and Qd6+.
games.quote: Threatening 27. [d7] followed by [Qd6+] …
games.source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 18, note to White's 26th move (QR-Q1); Olland – Alekhine, Scheveningen 1913, after 26.Rad1

claim: White has a protected passed pawn.
games.quote: White has a protected Passed Pawn and his Rook cuts the Black King off; hence, White is bound to attack.
games.source: Emanuel Lasker, Lasker's Manual of Chess (1927), rook-ending diagram 'White, Capablanca to play'; Capablanca – Tartakower, New York 1924, after 34...gxf5

claim: Black's rook dominates the only open file.
games.quote: In the present game Black has very evident compensations: (1) the greater mobility of the Black King, the adverse King being hampered by his own Pawns. (2) the dominating position of the Black Rook on the only open file.
games.source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 60, note to Black's 23rd move (23...Q-B6!), describing the ending reached after 24.Q-B1 QxQ 25.RxQ R-Q1; Yates – Alekhine, The Hague 1921, after 25...Rd8

claim: White's rook on the seventh cuts the Black king off.
games.quote: White has a protected Passed Pawn and his Rook cuts the Black King off; hence, White is bound to attack.
games.source: Emanuel Lasker, Lasker's Manual of Chess (1927), rook-ending diagram 'White, Capablanca to play'; Capablanca – Tartakower, New York 1924, after 34...gxf5

claim: White dominates the centre.
games.quote: White dominates the centre, but Black wants to simplify his game by [...e5] and to regain a share of the centre.
games.source: Emanuel Lasker, Lasker's Manual of Chess (1927), Bogoljubow v. Romanowski (Reti Opening), note to Black's 10th move; Bogoljubow – Romanovsky, Leningrad match 1924, after 10...Nbd7

claim: Black has the superiority in the centre.
games.quote: Black is well developed, he has the superiority in the centre and is aggressive on the Queen’s side.
games.source: Emanuel Lasker, Lasker's Manual of Chess (1927), Zukertort v. Steinitz (13th game of the match), note to Black's 24th move; Zukertort – Steinitz, World Championship 1886, after 24...Rac7

claim: Black permanently holds the centre: d5 is secured.
Black's d5 is definitely secured.
games.quote: Permanently taking hold of the centre, as his [d5] is definitely secured. From the strategic point of view this consideration is of paramount importance.
games.source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 12, note to Black's 16th move; Bernstein – Alekhine, Vilna 1912, after 16...f5

claim: Black has the better game with his two bishops.
Black's knight on e4 is strongly posted in the centre.
games.quote: Now Black has undoubtedly the better game, with his two Bishops and his strongly-posted Knight in the centre.
games.source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 96, note to Black's 9th move; Torres – Alekhine, Seville 1922, after 9...d5

claim: The two bishops are a decisive advantage for White.
games.quote: The loss of the present game by Black can be attributed to the fact that his Knights lack bases in the centre, and that in positions of this character the possession of the two Bishops constitutes a decisive advantage for the opponent.
games.source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 90 (match, Berlin 1921), note to White's 17th move; Alekhine – Teichmann, Berlin 1921, after 17.c3

claim: In this open position two bishops beat bishop and knight.
games.quote: In an open position such as this, two Bishops are more powerful than a Bishop and Knight.
games.source: Mason, The Principles of Chess (1894), Master Play, Evans Gambit, Martinez v. Zukertort, note to White's 23rd move; Martinez – Zukertort, Philadelphia 1884, after 23.Re1

claim: Black is forced to weaken his king-side still more.
games.quote: Now the threat of 27. [f4] … forces Black to weaken his King-side still more.
games.source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 37, note to White's 26th move; Alekhine – von Freymann, Cologne 1911, after 26...f6

claim: White's king is exposed; Black's is safely entrenched behind his pawns.
games.quote: Moreover, White's King is rather exposed while Black's King is safely entrenched behind his Pawns.
games.source: Edward Lasker, Chess and Checkers: The Way to Mastership (1918), Illustrative Game No. 1, note after White's 21st move (Diagram 68); Showalter – Ed. Lasker, Western Championship, Lexington 1917, after 21.Kg2

claim: White's king is exposed and Black takes the initiative.
games.quote: The text-move, just as 11. [Kf1] (Réti—Bogoljuboff, Berlin, 1920) is insufficient, in view of the exposed position of his King. Black at once assumes the initiative and keeps it to the end.
games.source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 26, note to White's 11th move; Tarrasch – Alekhine, St Petersburg 1914, after 11.Kd2

claim: White has a passed pawn and a commanding king.
games.quote: White not only has a passed Pawn, but his King is in a commanding position in the centre of the board ready to support the advance of White's Pawns, or, if necessary, to go to [c5], or to move to the right wing in case of danger.
games.source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), ch. V, §29, Example 61, note after White's 10th move (game move 36); Capablanca – Janowski, New York 1913, after 36.Rxg5

claim: Black has three isolated pawns, one attacked now and d6 next.
games.quote: He has three isolated Pawns, one of which is now attacked, another ([d6]) will be attacked next move.
games.source: Znosko-Borovsky, The Middle Game in Chess (1922), Inferiority in Force, Diagram LXVI, note to White's 4th move (game move 46); Schlechter – Lasker, World Championship match (game 1) 1910, after 46.Ne7

claim: Black's pawns are isolated and must be defended by pieces.
games.quote: He is two Pawns down for all practical purposes, and the Pawns he has are isolated and have to be defended by pieces.
games.source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), Part II, Game 7, note to Black's 34th move; Capablanca – Burn, San Sebastian 1911, after 34...Ke7

claim: Black's doubled c-pawn is a disadvantage he cannot undo.
games.quote: Black's game has the disadvantage of his double [c-pawn], which, to make matters worse, he cannot advance, because as soon as Black plays [...b6], White replies [b4].
games.source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), ch. V, §29, Example 61 (introductory note to the diagram); Capablanca – Janowski, New York 1913, after 26...Re8

claim: Black's extra pawn is doubled and of no account.
games.quote: Black has an extra pawn on the Queen's side. But as it is doubled, the material superiority is of no account.
games.source: Edward Lasker, Chess Strategy (1915), End-games from Master Play, I, Diag. 82; Teichmann – Blackburne, Berlin 1897, after 50...Ke6

claim: Black's isolated d5 pawn is weak and subject to attack.
games.quote: The drawback to the text move is that it leaves Black's [d5 pawn] isolated, and consequently weak and subject to attack.
games.source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), Part II, Game 9, note to Black's 13th move; Capablanca – Teichmann, Berlin 1913, after 13...Nxc5

claim: Black's isolated h7 pawn is weak.
games.quote: (4) Black's [h7 pawn] is isolated and therefore weak.
games.source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 78, note to Black's 20th move; Alekhine – Tartakower, Vienna 1922, after 20...Rxc8

claim: White commands the seventh rank.
games.quote: A glance at the position shows (1) that White commands the 7th Row; (2) that White's [e3 pawn] is isolated and his [g2 pawn] backward.
games.source: Nimzowitsch, My System (1930), Illustrative Game 10, note after Black's 35th move; Nimzowitsch – Tarrasch, Breslau 1925, after 35...Re6

claim: Black's rook on a2 is quite out of play.
games.quote: Before trying to push home his advantage on the Queen’s side, which is made possible by the weakness of White’s [d3 pawn], Black should look after his King’s side, where White has collected an alarming array of forces. After the text move the Rook is quite out of play.
games.source: Edward Lasker, Chess Strategy (1915), Game No. 48, note to Black's 24th move (R-R7); Blackburne – Nimzowitsch, St Petersburg 1914, after 24...Ra2

claim: Black's apparent queenside space is not real: his advanced pawns are targets.
games.quote: The number of moves and pieces is equal on both sides and we might look on Black as having an advantage in space on the Queen's wing. We know, however, that in reality the latter is not the case.
games.source: Znosko-Borovsky, The Middle Game in Chess (1922), Inferior Positions, Inferiority in Time, Diagram LXVII; Maróczy – Tarrasch, San Sebastian 1911, after 20.Nxg5

claim: Keeping the two bishops is a mistake for Black: the b7 bishop is inactive.
games.quote: Black aims at the exchange of Queens in order to remain with two Bishops for the ending, but in this position such a course is a mistake, because the Bishop on [b7] is inactive and cannot come into the game by any means, unless Black gives up the isolated Queen's Pawn which the Bishop must defend.
games.source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), Game 9, note to Black's 17th move; Capablanca – Teichmann, Berlin 1913, after 17...Qc4

claim: White's d5 knight cannot be maintained there.
games.quote: This Knight, as will be seen in the sequel, cannot be maintained in this position and will soon be exchanged against a Black piece inactive until now.
games.source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 60, note to White's 16th move; Yates – Alekhine, The Hague 1921, after 16.Nd5
